title: How Commercial Jingles Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore commercial jingles: what they are, how "audio branding" has supplanted them, the Wheaties Quartet as an early jingle, the 1930s origins of radio advertising, why jingles stick (repetition, rhyme, earworms and the phonological loop), a "playlist from Hell" of earworms, and the shift to licensing pop songs for ads (Nick Drake and VW, Nike and the Beatles, Sting refusing a deodorant ad, Black Keys vs. Pizza Hut, Band of Horses and Chevy). The episode closes with listener mail about Free IT Athens, a nonprofit that refurbishes donated computers.

segments.title: Opening banter and celebrity chatter
segments.summary: Hosts open with video-recording remarks, mention Mystery Science Theater alumni Joel Hodgson and Mike, and talk about Barry Manilow, Lynn Duddy, Jim Brickman, and royalty rights for jingles, plus a Manilow concert anecdote.

segments.title: Defining the commercial jingle and audio branding
segments.summary: Chuck defines a jingle as a snippet of memorable melody about a product, which can include a slogan, phone number, or call letters. They contrast jingles with audio branding or audio logos such as the NBC chimes, and mention the LG dryer melody and benefit-touting jingles like the Crest ads.

segments.title: Origins: Wheaties Quartet and In My Merry Oldsmobile
segments.summary: The Wheaties Quartet is credited with the first jingle, which reportedly saved Wheaties when radio play boosted sales. The hosts note a 1905 song, In My Merry Oldsmobile, that Oldsmobile used in the thirties; an article describes it as the first pop song licensed for commercial use rather than a true jingle.

segments.title: 1930s radio advertising and the rise of sponsored programming
segments.summary: Consumer protection rules limited direct advertising in the 1930s. Advertisers bought whole radio program time, producing shows like the King Biscuit Flower Hour and sponsored mysteries, which eventually led to modern radio and TV programming. Early ads were dry and bullet-pointed until jingles made an impact.

segments.title: Why jingles stick: earworms and the phonological loop
segments.summary: Simple, repetitive, rhyming jingles stick in memory, illustrated by the Oscar Mayer bologna song and a Seinfeld callback. Earworms are explained, and Baddeley and Hitch's working memory model with the phonological loop is described as the mechanism earworms exploit. Professor Colarusso's research is mentioned, along with tips for getting rid of earworms.

segments.title: Playlist from Hell and sports radio jingles
segments.summary: Colarusso's playlist from Hell is discussed, including Chili's baby back ribs jingle, Who Let the Dogs Out, We Will Rock You, Mission Impossible theme, YMCA, The Lion Sleeps Tonight, and It's a Small World. The hosts also discuss repetitive sports radio ads and a Blue Bell ice cream ad.

segments.title: Licensing pop songs and celebrity ad controversies
segments.summary: Companies increasingly license existing pop songs instead of writing jingles: VW used Nick Drake's Pink Moon, Nike used the Beatles' Revolution, and Jaguar's use of Don't Stand So Close to Me was refused by Sting. Band of Horses licensed a song to Chevy, and the Black Keys sued Pizza Hut over a song resembling Gold on the Ceiling. Ray Parker Junior lost a case over I Need a New Drug, and the hosts note the rise of soundalike remakes.

segments.title: Product placement and Soap Opera Cereal
segments.summary: The hosts note that DVRs make product placement more common and mention a viral YouTube parody called Soap Opera Cereal that is over-the-top product placement.

segments.title: Listener mail: Free IT Athens
segments.summary: A listener from Athens, Georgia, promotes Free IT Athens, a volunteer nonprofit that refurbishes donated laptops and computers for low-income people and recycles e-waste. Financial donations are also accepted via freeitathens.org.

segments.title: Sign-off and how to get in touch
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to submit commercial jingles and ways to contact the show via Twitter, Facebook, and email, and point to HowStuffWorks for more.
